source: Puech, Macina, Chatain, Sachan, Kapur (2025) Towards the Pedagogical Steering of LLMs for Tutoring: A Case Study with Modeling Productive Failure (StratL), ACL Findings
finding: First system to make an LLM tutor (GPT-4o) follow a productive failure strategy. StratL traces the student state, picks a pedagogical intent from a hand-built graph, then writes a steering prompt. Without it the LLM tutor gives away solutions.
numbers: Simulated students, 3 conversations x 2 problems x 4 versions. Mean student-generated solution methods (RSMs) on the invention problem: StratL 2.34, no-intent baseline 1.0, constant-intent 1.34, LLM-chosen intent 1.34. PF Score (0-4) on Consistency / Country: StratL 3.67 / 4.00, baseline 1.33 / 0.44, LLM-chosen 3.67 / 3.11.
quote: most models often reveal the solution of the exercise to the students, even if prompted not to
limits: Measures PF fidelity only, not learning gains. Simulated students in the preliminary study. Only school math.
agent_relevance: Default instruction-tuned LLMs do not hold back help. If our agent must attempt before being told, the order has to be enforced by the scaffold, not requested in a prompt.

source: Puech et al. (2025) StratL, ablation: who chooses the intent
finding: Letting the LLM pick the tutoring intent from a plain-language description of PF was not enough. A hand-written selection graph worked better.
numbers: PF Score on Country problem: hand-built graph 4.00 vs LLM-selected intent 3.11 vs no-intent 0.44. RSMs: 2.34 vs 1.34 vs 1.0. Student state tracing micro F1 = 0.77 (10 conversations per problem, one annotator).
quote: providing a natural language description of the tutoring strategy ... does not yield satisfactory results
limits: Small simulation (3 runs per cell). State tracing is only 0.77 F1, so wrong labels cause contradictory intents.
agent_relevance: A phase-order rule (attempt, then reveal) should be code or a state machine in our schema (S-states), not a sentence the model interprets.

source: Puech et al. (2025) StratL, field test
finding: With 17 Singapore 9th graders, the steered tutor got students to produce more partial solutions. Students rated the unsteered tutor as more helpful.
numbers: N=17, 15 minutes each. StratL PF score higher, p=.046 (2-sample t) on Consistency. Student RSMs about 2.6 under StratL vs lower under baseline, p=.05. Helpfulness (of 3) Consistency: StratL 1.20 vs baseline 2.00; Country 2.67 vs 2.80. Coherence 1.80 vs 2.25 (n.s.).
quote: students spend more time being stuck and exploring suboptimal solutions
limits: Tiny N, no learning outcome, rating n per cell 3-5. Students complained the tutor ignored valid alternative solutions.
agent_relevance: Holding back help lowers felt helpfulness. In an agent loop the cost is extra turns and a risk of ignoring a valid off-path solution; add a check that accepts any correct attempt.

source: Rotter, Benazet i Montobbio, Hernandez-Leo (2026) Access Timing as Scaffolding: An RL Approach to GenAI in Education, arXiv 2605.15850
finding: An RL agent decided when students could use off-the-shelf GenAI, with a reward built on productive failure (reward access after struggle). Timed access beat always-on access on post-test and metacognitive accuracy, and matched no access.
numbers: N=105 (Always 36, RL 37, Never 32). Post-test RL vs Always t(71)=2.51, p=.014, d=0.59. RL vs Never t(67)=-0.30, p=.762, d=-0.07. Metacognitive accuracy RL vs Always d=0.54, p=.023; RL vs Never d=0.07. Mean AI requests: Always 11.25, RL 2.46, Never 0. Metacognitive gain by condition: F(2,87)=0.86, p=.425 (H3 rejected).
quote: no studies to ... productive failure and GenAI
limits: Lab study, single session. RL policy trained on only 9 interactions. Never condition was as good as RL, so benefit is vs unrestricted use, not vs no AI. Fewer-mistakes effect vs Never (d=0.51, p=.047) vanished after controlling gender.
agent_relevance: Evidence that WHEN help arrives matters more than WHETHER it exists. Supports gating lesson retrieval until after a first attempt in our loop.

source: Suriyaarachchi, Denny, Nanayakkara (2025) Investigating the Use of Productive Failure ... Introductory Python Programming, SIGCSE TS
finding: PF versus direct instruction for Python lists in programming (a code domain). Same immediate success after the lesson, better success two weeks later for PF. Cognitive load (heart-rate variability) fell more after PF instruction.
numbers: N=20 (DI 9, PF 7 analysed in the table). Table 1 successes: DI weather task 8/9, heart-rate task 8/9, two-week delayed heart-rate task 6/9. PF weather task (attempted before instruction) 2/7, heart-rate task 7/7, delayed heart-rate task 7/7.
limits: Very small sample, no inferential test reported in the text read, one concept, a novel sensor task. Fidelity of PF design uncertain.
agent_relevance: Programming is the closest domain to code agents. Suggests the first attempt fails but the post-lesson solution persists; a model-free analogue is storing lessons only after a failed attempt.

source: Sinha and Kapur (2021) When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure, Review of Educational Research 91(5)
finding: Meta-analysis of problem solving then instruction (PS-I) vs instruction then problem solving (I-PS). Moderate overall benefit of PS-I, larger for high-fidelity PF designs. Reversals for young children and domain-general skills.
numbers: 53 studies, 166 comparisons. Hedges g=0.36 [0.20, 0.51]. High-fidelity PF g 0.37 to 0.58. Publication-bias-adjusted g=0.87. Moderators: grade level, time span, (quasi-)experimental design. Grades 2-5 and domain-general skills favoured I-PS.
limits: Read via search summary and OpenAlex abstract only. Adjusted g=0.87 is a model-dependent estimate and larger than the raw effect, so treat as uncertain.
agent_relevance: Effect is moderate, not huge. Expect a modest gain from attempt-first in an agent and a possible reversal on easy or generic skills.

source: Sinha and Kapur (2021) From problem-solving to sensemaking: comparative meta-analysis of preparatory approaches (ETH Research Collection)
finding: Compared PS-I with scaffolded PS-I and with a sensemaking activity before instruction. Scaffolding added nothing detectable. PS-I over sensemaking not significant.
numbers: 118 comparisons, 33 articles. PS-I vs +PS-I g=-0.08 [-0.20, 0.04]; Bayesian: 99% probability the difference is under 0.2. PS-I vs !PS-I (sensemaking) g=0.22 [-0.06, 0.51]; 40.37% probability of a moderate effect. Bias-adjusted g=0.55 and 0.64.
limits: Working-paper page, abstract-level data. Sensemaking comparison is weak evidence either way.
agent_relevance: The step that matters may be preparatory activity of any kind before the lesson, not failure itself. A cheap structured pre-lesson step may do the job.

source: Kapur (2011) Designing for Productive Failure, Journal of the Learning Sciences (also Kapur 2009 quasi-experiments on average speed)
finding: Seventh-grade classes solved complex average-speed problems with no support and failed, then received teacher consolidation. They beat direct-instruction classes on well-structured and higher-order application items. A second school with lower-ability students replicated it.
numbers: Two quasi-experimental studies in 3 Singapore public schools; exact N and effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only via OpenAlex. Quasi-experimental, intact classes.
agent_relevance: Founding pattern: failure in the attempt phase is expected and does not predict poor outcomes.

source: Kapur, Saba, Roll (2023) Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure, npj Science of Learning
finding: The number of different solution methods students invent during the attempt predicts the posttest far better than prior achievement or prior topic knowledge.
numbers: Two quasi-experiments, N=112 (grade 7 ratios) and 105 (grade 8 variance). RSMs on posttest: F(1,107)=62.59 and F(1,100)=105.52, both p<.001. Prerequisite knowledge p=.102 and .484. School RSM gap d=0.48 then d=0.03.
limits: No direct-instruction group. Two schools. RSMs counted per group.
agent_relevance: Our analogue: count distinct candidate solutions the agent generates before the lesson. Diversity of attempts is the thing to measure and to force (this ties to the diversity target in the schema).

source: Authors not verified (2020) When failure fails to be productive: probing PF beyond STEM, Instructional Science
finding: Failed replication in a non-STEM domain. PF students did not beat direct-instruction students when learning social science research methods.
numbers: Two quasi-experiments, N=212 and N=152 tenth graders. No PF advantage.
limits: Abstract only. Authors not verified from the abstract. Quasi-experimental.
agent_relevance: Boundary: the effect may not hold for tasks without a canonical, discoverable structure. Do not apply attempt-first to every task type.

source: Authors not verified (2020) The effect of contrasting cases during problem solving prior to and after instruction, Instructional Science
finding: Merely delaying instruction did not raise conceptual understanding. Instruction first gave better procedural fluency. Contrasting cases did not help.
numbers: N=181, mean age 14.53, 2x2 design (order x contrasting cases). Instruction-first students made fewer but higher-quality solution attempts.
limits: Abstract only. Single experiment.
agent_relevance: The order swap alone is not the active ingredient. Procedural tasks may favour lesson-first, so the gate should depend on whether we want conceptual or procedural gains.

source: Robust effects of explicit failure-driven scaffolding in problem-solving prior to instruction: a replication and extension (2021), Learning and Instruction
finding: Controlled experiment comparing failure-driven, success-driven, and no scaffolding before instruction. Posttest similar for non-isomorphic items, but failure-driven gave higher reasoning quality and better transfer.
numbers: Posttest scores similar across groups on conceptual items; transfer benefit for failure-driven in scores and reasoning quality (exact N not read).
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Designing the attempt to expose gaps (failure) beats designing it for easy success, which supports prompts that stress-test the first attempt.

source: Shinn, Cassano, Berman, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: Agents attempt a task, fail, write a verbal self-reflection, store it in memory, and retry. This is a machine version of failure then lesson.
numbers: ALFWorld: ReAct+Reflexion solved 130 of 134 tasks over 12 trials, absolute +22%; plain ReAct plateaued between trials 6 and 7. HotPotQA +20%. HumanEval Python up to +11%. Baselines ReAct, CoT and CoT(GT) fixed no failed task on retry at temperature 0.7.
limits: Needs a reliable success signal. Memory is a sliding window. WebShop: no improvement after 4 trials, reflections not helpful.
agent_relevance: Closest existing method to 'lessons after first attempt'. Gains depend on the retry loop and an external pass/fail signal.

source: Reflexion ablations (Shinn et al. 2023, sections 4.2-4.3)
finding: The written reflection step is the active part. Removing the natural-language explanation after failure gave no gain over baseline; removing test generation lowered score.
numbers: HotPotQA CoT(GT): self-reflection gives an 8% absolute boost over just keeping the last trajectory (episodic memory). HumanEval Rust hardest 50 with GPT-4: no internal tests 52% vs 60% full. Omitting the explanation step did not improve over baseline.
limits: Small subsets (50 problems; 100 HotPotQA questions). Single model family.
agent_relevance: Store an explained lesson, not the raw failed trace. Supports 'lesson after attempt' over 'keep the transcript'.

source: Zhao, Huang, Xu, Lin, Liu, Huang (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners, AAAI
finding: Agent tries training tasks, collects successes and failures, extracts natural-language insights by comparing failed and successful attempts, then retrieves insights and successful examples on unseen tasks with one try.
numbers: HotpotQA success: ReAct 28.0, hand-crafted insights 32.0, insights built with reflections 29.0, gpt-3.5 insights 32.0, ExpeL 39.0. ALFWorld: ReAct 40.0, random examples 42.5, reasoning-similarity retrieval 48.5, ExpeL 59.0. Insights-only vs retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%.
limits: Text-only environments. WebShop gain smaller. Quality of insights depends on base model.
agent_relevance: A cross-task version of the PF lesson step: failed-vs-successful comparison is what yields the lesson. Learning from success pairs plus failures beats either alone.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL, comparison with Reflexion and synergy
finding: Cross-task insights with a single attempt matched in-task retries, and the two combined best.
numbers: ALFWorld by round R0 to R3: ReAct+Reflexion 40.3, 47.8, 52.2, 54.4; ExpeL retrieve-only 54.5, 57.5, 59.7, 60.4; ExpeL+Reflexion 59.0, 60.4, 63.4, 64.2. HotpotQA: ExpeL 40% at R3 vs Reflexion 39%.
limits: R1-R3 started from failed R0 checkpoints, so they are not a clean independent test.
agent_relevance: Lessons carried from earlier failures transfer to new tasks; retries add a smaller extra gain on top.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR
finding: Boundary condition for 'attempt then revise'. Without an outside label, asking the model to critique and fix its own answer makes it worse. Gains in earlier papers came from using oracle correctness labels.
numbers: With oracle labels, GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7; GPT-4 HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0. Without oracle: GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 (round 1) and 90.0 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 84.0 to 81.5. GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K and more often changed right to wrong than wrong to right.
limits: Intrinsic self-correction only; tested on GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA.
agent_relevance: Failure is only productive if the agent knows it failed. Our loop needs an external or verifier signal before writing a lesson (guardrail on false lessons).

source: Wang, Li, Han, Zhang, Baldwin (2024) Learning From Failure: Integrating Negative Examples when Fine-tuning LLMs as Agents
finding: Failed agent trajectories help training if marked as negative with a different prompt (NAT), but hurt if mixed in as if they were good (NUT). Gain is largest when positive data is scarce.
numbers: Math: NAT +8.74% with a 7B model and 2k positive examples; +0.52% with a 13B model and 5k positives. QA gains about 8% over no negatives and about 3% over NUT. With 2k positives plus 10k low-quality negatives the change was negative (about -3.1, text cut). CoT prompting math: +6.68% over vanilla.
limits: This is fine-tuning (weights), not a prompt scaffold. Zeng et al. 2023 found negatives harmful, so the sign depends on how they are labelled.
agent_relevance: For memory: label failures as failures. A lesson store that mixes failed attempts unlabelled can poison later runs.

source: Experiential Reflective Learning for Self-Improving LLM Agents (2026), arXiv 2603.24639
finding: Agent reflects on task trajectories and outcomes to write heuristics, retrieves relevant ones at test time and injects them into context.
numbers: Gaia2 benchmark: success rate +7.8% over a ReAct baseline.
limits: Abstract only via OpenAlex.
agent_relevance: Recent confirmation that retrieved post-attempt heuristics give a modest gain (about 8 points) rather than a large one.

source: Small vs. Large Language Models: Comparing LMs in Generating Productive Failure Math Problems (2026), ICLS proceedings / EdArXiv
finding: LLMs can write PF tasks. GPT-4o wrote better PF problems than the small model Phi-3 on five rater dimensions.
numbers: 60 problems (30 per model), matched on grade, Common Core standard, theme, interest, prior knowledge. GPT-4o M=13.38 (SD 1.88) vs Phi-3 M=10.67 (SD 2.73), d=1.16.
limits: Rater scores, no student learning outcome. Full PDF unavailable (repository error); abstract read via OSF API.
agent_relevance: The agent can generate its own hard first-attempt tasks, but quality depends on model size. Small models give weaker practice problems.

source: Oreopoulos, Liut, Sungu, Low (2026) Making AI Tutoring Productive: Evidence from a Mastery-Based Math Practice Experiment, NBER WP 35621
finding: Large RCT of AI support for math practice. AI helped after mistakes but slowed progress; delayed learning gains were weak and only marginal when AI was combined with a mastery workflow.
numbers: 6,000+ middle-school students; randomised on AI vs no AI, mastery vs non-mastery, topic. AI students attempted fewer questions but answered more accurately per attempt. Delayed test one week later: mastery alone did not raise delayed learning; marginally significant gains on practiced material with AI plus mastery. No effect sizes on the page.
limits: Abstract page only; magnitudes not given. Not a PF test.
agent_relevance: Structure around the mistake decides whether AI help is productive. Supports an explicit error-handling step rather than free-flowing help.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS (as summarised in a search result)
finding: About 1,000 Turkish high-school maths students. Unrestricted LLM access raised practice performance but lowered later unaided exam results; a guardrailed tutor largely avoided the harm.
numbers: N about 1,000 (from a secondary summary; exact effects not verified). Page returned HTTP 403.
limits: Secondary source only; not verified.
agent_relevance: Closest large-scale human evidence of 'unproductive success' from early LLM help, the opposite of attempt-first.

source: Cross-reading of c01-c03 and c17: PF steering vs self-correction
finding: Two separate problems show up. LLMs do not delay help on their own (c01), and they cannot tell when their own attempt failed (c17). Both must be supplied from outside the model.
numbers: StratL RSMs 2.34 vs 1.0 baseline; self-correct without oracle lowers GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 for GPT-4-Turbo.
limits: Synthesis across different settings (tutoring vs reasoning).
agent_relevance: Design note: gate (attempt before lesson) plus verifier (know it failed) are separate parts of the scaffold.

source: Rotter et al. (2026) reward design of the access-timing RL agent
finding: The RL reward encoded productive failure as: reward access after a struggle, penalise access before any effort, and penalise prolonged unproductive struggle. This is a computational PF rule.
numbers: Policy trained from n=9 prior interactions; student AI requests fell from 11.25 (Always) to 2.46 (RL).
limits: Reward weights come from theory, tuned on a very small pilot.
agent_relevance: A usable rule for our agent: allow the lesson after a minimum attempt, and cap how long it may keep failing before the lesson is released.

source: Suriyaarachchi et al. (2025) Python PF study, pilot design and interpretations
finding: The authors link the DI group's delayed errors to 'unproductive success' and PF's persistence to prior-knowledge activation during the attempt. Pilot: think-aloud with 11 students to tune the task.
numbers: DI: 3 of 9 failed the delayed task (two had passed earlier, one had never passed). PF: 0 of 7 failed.
limits: Interpretation is the authors' own, untested mechanism. n tiny.
agent_relevance: Mechanism worth testing in the agent: does a failed first attempt change what it retrieves from its own knowledge?

source: Reflexion limitation: creative local minima (Shinn et al. 2023, section 6)
finding: Reflection loops get stuck when escape needs very creative behaviour. On WebShop with a two-shot ReAct+Reflexion agent in 100 environments, runs were stopped after 4 trials with no sign of improvement.
numbers: 100 WebShop environments, 4 trials, no improvement.
limits: Authors' own report; one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Lessons from a failed attempt narrow the search toward the same family of solutions. Pair with a diversity step (many attempts) as PF does with solution methods.

source: Kapur and colleagues (2014) Productive failure in learning the concept of variance / math, Cognitive Science (abstract via search)
finding: Two randomised controlled studies: both methods give high procedural knowledge, but students who problem-solved before instruction showed more conceptual understanding and transfer. The number of student-generated solutions predicted learning.
numbers: Exact N and effect sizes not obtained (search summary only).
limits: Not opened; numbers missing.
agent_relevance: Same driver as c09: count of generated solutions.
